thread.title: An Ethanol Pair Trade That Offers A Return Of 25% Or More: REX American Resources And Pacific Ethanol - Pacific Ethanol, (NASDAQ:PEIX)

author: Tristan R. Brown
title: An Ethanol Pair Trade That Offers A Return Of 25% Or More: REX American Resources And Pacific Ethanol - Pacific Ethanol, (NASDAQ:PEIX)
text:
Overview of Investment Thesis
Pacific Ethanol ( PEIX ) and REX American Resources ( REX ) are two very different independent U.S. producers of corn ethanol. Pacific Ethanol is one of the country's larger independent producers with ethanol facilities on the West Coast and, more recently following a major acquisition, the Midwest. The company has struggled to achieve positive profit margins over the last several years, and its heavy debt load has negatively impacted its financial returns over the last year as U.S. ethanol demand has weakened. REX, on the other hand, is a small producer that has historically focused on strong margins over revenue growth. The company has no long-term debt and a large cash position, two factors that have contributed to its ability to routinely report much higher profit margins than its independent peers.
The share prices of both companies have turned sharply lower since early 2017 as the ethanol sector's operating conditions have deteriorated, although that of REX has held up well relative to that of Pacific Ethanol. The ethanol sector now finds itself facing substantial national policy uncertainty with regard to the future of the U.S. biofuels mandate even as a declining gasoline price has caused ethanol production margins to fall to zero. Some analysts and industry observers believe that the Trump administration, which has actively weakened the blending mandate and demand for ethanol since early 2017, will reverse course in an effort to woo Midwestern voters prior to the 2020 presidential election. Market signals, on the other hand, continue to forecast an extended period of low ethanol production margins.
The challenge facing investors is how to gain exposure to the possibility of higher ethanol producer share prices in the event that the Trump administration strengthens the mandate but while minimizing downside risk in the event that the status quo is maintained. Both outcomes can be expected to have a large impact on the share prices of both Pacific Ethanol and, to a lesser extent, REX. This article presents a pair trade in which investors initiate a long position in REX that is hedged via a short position in Pacific Ethanol. The proposed trade is structured so that investors will achieve a return of 25% or more if the Trump administration reverses course on the biofuels mandate but will have their losses limited in the event that the status quo is maintained.
Background
U.S. ethanol producer Green Plains, Inc. ( GPRE ) announced earlier this month that it is permanently shuttering its Hopewell, Virginia ethanol facility. Unlike the temporary production shutdown that occurred at the company's Superior, Iowa and Lakota, Iowa facilities in September prior to the Lakota facility's sale to Valero Energy ( VLO ) the following month, the Hopewell facility is to be decommissioned and dismantled. This brings the amount by which Green Plains has reduced its ethanol production capacity in Q4 to date alone to 340 million gallons, or almost 25% of its total capacity in Q3. While the Hopewell decision was likely made weeks ago, the fact that the price of gasoline has declined by 20% since the sale of the other facilities was announced can only have reinforced management's choice (see figure).
GPRE data by YCharts The ethanol industry's operating environment has remained dismal in Q4 as its margins have hovered right around zero. Green Plains has shed ethanol assets in response to this environment as part of its "strategic shift" away from that sector and towards the more lucrative feed ingredients sector. That the Hopewell facility is being decommissioned rather than temporarily idled or sold shows just how dismal Green Plains expects ethanol margins to remain in the quarters ahead. It also demonstrates the intensity of management's focus on ignoring sunk costs in favor of a rapid reduction to its ethanol sector exposure. The statement about the shuttering comes just over three years after Green Plains announced that it was purchasing the Hopewell facility as part of its then-transformation into one of the country's largest ethanol producers. The acquisition came with a $25 million price tag after upgrades, and Hopewell resumed full production in Q3 2016. The facility had long struggled to be profitable under its previous ownership due to its lack of access to cheap Midwestern corn, though, and Green Plains was apparently unable to make it profitable enough to sell under prevailing operating conditions. The facility will ultimately be cannibalized for parts that will be sent to the company's remaining ethanol facilities.
The takeaway for investors from these two announcements by Green Plains is that not all ethanol facilities are equal in the current operating environment. Some, such as the Hopewell facility, are more or less worthless. Others, such as the facilities that were sold to Valero, continue to be valuable even amid an extended period of low production margins. This has important implications for how investors should value different ethanol producers. The next section discusses how this dynamic affects the valuation of one of the sector's lower-margin independent producers, Pacific Ethanol, and why this makes a short position in the company a useful hedge against a long position in the ethanol sector.
The long thesis: REX American Resources
REX American Resources is the ethanol sector's version of Apple ( AAPL ) in that it has historically pursued margins over volumes. It is one of the sector's smallest publicly-traded producers with annual production of no more than 270 million gallons based on owned annual capacity of 261 million gallons (this latter number has fluctuated a bit over the years). This lack of capacity has allowed the company to focus on maximizing its operating efficiencies and margins, however, with the result being a post-2014 average EBITDA/gallon that is almost equal to the sector's average margins for the same period (see table). In fact, the margins of REX American Resources have sometimes surpassed the sector's, such as in 2016 and 2015. The company owns stakes in six different ethanol facilities (see second table). It also recently acquired a refined coal segment that provides valuable Section 45 tax credits .

Management's focus on making the company one of the sector's most profitable small operators has enabled it to take excellent care of its balance sheet. As importantly, the company did not follow the path of expansion that was adopted by both Green Plains and Pacific Ethanol after fuel prices fell sharply in 2014. This decision has had a very positive impact on its investors: whereas Green Plains is rolling back its expansion and Pacific Ethanol is still struggling with the debt load that it obtained from its expansion, REX instead spent the years after 2014 eliminating its long-term debt, reducing its current liabilities, and expanding its cash reserve (see figure). This year it found itself in the position of being able to repurchase large numbers of shares, and its current authorization is equal to 7% of its share outstanding. I would not be surprised if management announces in its upcoming earnings report an expansion of this buyback program given continued share price weakness.
REX Total Long Term Debt (Quarterly) data by YCharts The share price of REX American Resources has fallen by nearly 20% in 2018 to date as the sector's conditions have worsened, although it has strongly outperformed that of Pacific Ethanol (see figure). The former's best-in-class margins have also allowed it to avoid much of the volatility that has affected the share prices of its peers. A consequence of REX's earnings strength in recent quarters is that its trailing EV/EBITDA ratio has steadily declined to 7.4x despite the backstop provided by its cash reserve and buyback program (see second figure). This decline has accelerated as bearishness in the petroleum markets has grown more pronounced since Q3, which is why REX's valuation has declined even as its earnings have held up well relative to expectations.
REX data by YCharts REX EV to EBITDA ( TTM ) data by YCharts REX's low valuation fails to account for the possibility of one or more major policy shifts occurring in 2019. While I do not consider either to be guaranteed to occur, I do categorize each of them as high impact individual events. My lack of certainty with regard to whether or not even one of the policy shifts will occur relates to the policy-driven nature of the U.S. ethanol market, in which demand is driven as much by federal policymaking (and politics) as it is by market forces such as the price of gasoline. The first, and largest, possible impact is that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency [EPA] reverses course by restoring the actual blending volume allowed for corn ethanol to 15 billion gallons. A major reason for the ethanol sector's current difficulties is the EPA's Q2 decision to effectively reduce that number to 14 billion gallons (and more than one industry observer has told me that the more realistic number is 13 billion gallons) by awarding widespread " hardship waivers " to U.S. refiners. This decision has contributed to the ethanol sector's current glut and comparatively low ethanol prices.
Some industry observers expect that this decision will be reversed in 2019 as part of the Trump administration's re-election calculus, causing ethanol demand and, by extension, prices and production margins, to rebound. The logic runs as follows: President Donald Trump won the 2016 presidential election by capturing Midwestern swing states. The economies of these states rely heavily on agricultural production, of which corn is a mainstay. If President Trump has any intention of winning the 2020 presidential election then he will need to bring those states back to his side even after his party lost many of them in the recent midterm elections. The simplest way to do this would be to stop the (probably illegal, according to an appellate court opinion that was written by the most recent appointee to the U.S. Supreme Court) mass handouts of hardship waivers to refiners. This is especially true now that the architects of the ethanol's mandate's weakening, former White House adviser Carl Icahn and former EPA head Scott Pruitt, are no longer members of the Trump administration.
The second possible development is that President Trump restores positive trade relations with major ethanol markets such as China. That country was expected to be a major destination for U.S. ethanol due to its own blending mandate and lack of domestic ethanol production, both of which combined to make it one of America's largest ethanol trade partners at times between 2015 and 2017 (see figure). The Trump administration's decision to launch a trade war with China prompted the latter country to impose hefty tariffs on U.S. ethanol, however, prompting executives in the ethanol sector to state during their Q3 earnings call that the U.S. ethanol glut will persist so long as the Chinese market remains off-limits to them. The two countries' negotiators continue to work toward a compromise agreement on trade, however, and it is feasible that such an agreement would see the lifting of China's restrictions on U.S. ethanol imports.
Either development would have an immediate positive impact on REX's share price. More importantly, even the mere rumor that one or both developments was likely to occur, possibly sparked by a tweet from President Trump, would likely send the company's share price much higher. The share price has demonstrated substantial headline volatility in the past, including in response to President Trump's unexpected election victory in November 2016 (see figure). A more sustained rise, such as the 139% increase that the company's share price recorded in the first eight months of 2014 or the 83% increase that it recorded over the course of 2016, would also be possible in the event that one or both developments prompted a long-term improvement to the ethanol sector's production margins. Both developments are far from certain given that policy trends have moved in the opposite direction over the course of the Trump presidency, but their occurrence would have a very positive impact on the long thesis for REX.
REX data by YCharts The hedge - Pacific Ethanol
The main lesson that I have learned in a decade of studying the U.S. ethanol sector is to expect the unexpected from policy developments. This has been especially true during the Trump presidency, whether in the case of former Special Adviser to the President Carl Icahn's machinations involving the biofuels mandate in early 2017 or former EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt's subsequent successful attempts to partially roll the mandate back. REX American Resources has a great deal of appeal as a long investment opportunity due to its record of strong margins, lack of long-term debt, and large cash reserve. At the same time, though, I recognize that there is a substantial probability that the Trump administration will not take steps to re-strengthen the mandate in 2019 and/or negotiate a lifting of China's tariffs on U.S. ethanol, in which case the long thesis is less attractive. It is therefore important that long investors also have a hedge against the possibility that an improved policy environment does not materialize. Such a hedge is available in the form of a smaller short position in REX's much less profitable peer Pacific Ethanol.
In my opinion the investors that should be the most concerned about the Hopewell ethanol facility's decommissioning are those in Pacific Ethanol. The company has seen its share price shed almost 70% of its value in 2018 to date, and it now trades at a small fraction of its book value (see figure). The share price decline can be easily explained by the fact that Pacific Ethanol has long been the low-margin producer in the independent ethanol sector, a trait that has made it doubly unattractive in the low-margin operating environment that has prevailed across the entire sector this year. The incredibly low price/book ratio has prompted more debate, however, with some Seeking Alpha commenters arguing after Green Plains sold 20% of its capacity to Valero for an average of $1/gallon that this price meant that Pacific Ethanol's market capitalization was understating its market value.
PEIX data by YCharts My response was that the latter's inability to report a positive profit margin in five of the last six years made it difficult to accurately compare the value of that company's ethanol facilities with those of Green Plains. This week's announcement by Green Plains illustrates why: whereas the company received good value for its prime Midwestern facilities, its long-struggling East Coast facility is to effectively be scrapped for parts. This in turn suggests that Pacific Ethanol's long-struggling facilities, especially its unprofitable West Coast facilities, are worth far less than $1/gallon in the current market. It is instructive here to consider that Green Plains paid $0.42/gallon (including upgrades) for the Hopewell facility at a time when the ethanol crush spread averaged $0.21/gallon but is decommissioning it just three years later when the spread is averaging $0.02/gallon. 200 million gallons of Pacific Ethanol's 605 million gallons of ethanol capacity is located on or near the West Coast, and it obtained its more profitable Midwestern capacity for roughly $1/gallon in a quarter in which the crush spread was $0.57/gallon higher than it is now.
Here it is particularly instructive to compare Pacific Ethanol's historical profit margins with those of REX American Resources. Whereas REX focuses on operating a small production volume at a very high level of efficiency and profitability, Pacific Ethanol operates a larger production volume (605 million gallons in FY 2017) at a much lower level of profitability. REX's annual profit margins have been around 10 percentage points higher than those of Pacific Ethanol since 2014 as a result (see figure), and only the Midwestern drought of 2012 was able to cause it to report a net loss (and then just barely). REX's book value of $385.1 million implies ethanol production capacity value of $1.43/gallon, although in reality this is a bit lower at $1.38/gallon since REX's book value also includes the small refined coal operation that it purchased in Q2 2017 for $12 million in cash. By contrast, Pacific Ethanol's book value of $329.4 million implies an ethanol production capacity value of only $0.54/gallon.
PEIX Profit Margin (Annual) data by YCharts Book value alone provides an incomplete picture, however. Consider instead the two companies' TTM EBITDA/gallon results. At the end of Q2 (REX's earnings calendar lags that of Pacific Ethanol by one month so Q2 is the latest quarter for which both companies' data is available) Pacific Ethanol had a TTM EBITDA of $19 million , or $0.03/gallon of ethanol capacity. One month later REX had a TTM EBITDA also of $40 million but, due to its smaller size, the higher value of $0.15/gallon of ethanol capacity. Pacific Ethanol's result fell to $0.02/gallon at the end of Q3 and, while REX's corresponding value is likely to also be lower on a QoQ basis, it will also be substantially higher than that of Pacific Ethanol. This means that Pacific Ethanol's West Coast facilities have most likely been running on a negative EBITDA basis that is being offset, if only just, by its Midwest capacity from the Aventine acquisition.
Pacific Ethanol's West Coast capacity totals 200 million gallons and its Midwest capacity totals 405 million gallons. It is reasonable to assume that the West Coast capacity, which is unlikely to have been EBITDA-positive over the TTM period, is of a similar category as the Green Plains Hopewell facility in that it has little-to-no book value in the prevailing operating conditions. This would leave the Midwest capacity to justify the company's $329.4 million book value, giving it a value of $0.81/gallon. At first glance this might seem reasonable in light of the $1/gallon price that Green Plains received for the sale of its Midwest facilities to Valero. It would also imply a discount for Pacific Ethanol's Midwest capacity from the $1/gallon price that it paid for those facilities in Q4 2014, which is also reasonable at face value given that the sector's production margins averaged $0.44/gallon in that quarter. A second look shows the flaws in this logic, however.
Pacific Ethanol's adj. EBITDA/gallon should have improved relative to the sector's production margins after Q4 2014 based on the high price that it paid for the Aventine capacity. It did not. On the contrary, it has actually declined. Whereas the sector's annual average production margin fell by 44% between 2013 and 2017, Pacific Ethanol's adj. EBITDA/gallon fell by 60% over the same period (see table). Worse, the EBITDA/gallon result does not account for the costs that the company incurred in financing the deal in the form of higher interest expenses (Pacific Ethanol took on $145 million of Aventine's term debt) and shareholder dilution (Aventine shareholders received 1.25 shares of Pacific Ethanol's stock for every share of Aventine stock). After taking those additional costs into account it is clear why Pacific Ethanol has been unable to achieve positive profit margins for so many years. It also illustrates why Pacific Ethanol's Midwest capacity is unlikely to be purchased by a third party for even $0.81/gallon, let alone the $1/gallon that Green Plains recently received.

Pacific Ethanol's usefulness as a hedge against a long position in REX is based on the fact that corn ethanol operating conditions have deteriorated rapidly since the start of Q4. The sector's average production margin in the quarter to date has been $0.06/gallon, or 74% lower than in the first three months of the year (see figure). While ethanol prices do weaken at the end of the year as the driving season draws to a close, this year's average production margin for Q4 to date has been much worse than in previous years; 2016's comparable figure was $0.42/gallon and 2017's was $0.21/gallon, for example. This leads me to believe that Pacific Ethanol's Q4 EBITDA, which the consensus currently forecasts to be $6.1 million, or $0.01/gallon, will ultimately be very close to zero. This estimate is based on two factors. First, the company recorded an adj. EBITDA in Q3 of $0.04/gallon despite the sector's average production margin of $0.20/gallon for the same period. Second, in the closest post-Aventine analogue to current operating conditions, Pacific Ethanol recorded an EBITDA of less than $0.01/gallon in Q1 2016 when the sector's average margin was $0.04/gallon. Management's November 1 announcement that it had cut its production by 10% provides further support for this estimate.
Source: CARD (2018).
The poor numbers above notwithstanding, Pacific Ethanol's EBITDA results in 2018 to date have actually made its operating conditions appear better than they have been in reality. This is because the company has recorded a beneficial change to working capital of $21.1 million over the period that has had a positive impact on its operating cash flow. The working capital change has been due to a substantial reduction to its inventories and a smaller reduction to its accounts payable. Excluding changes to working capital, then, its operating cash flow in 2018 to date has been less than $5 million total, or $0.01/gallon. Pacific Ethanol, in other words, has been financing its operations this year through asset sales rather than through ethanol production. Its inventory sales have also occurred at a time when ethanol is trading at a decade low in both real and nominal terms (see figure), meaning that its recent earnings performance was effectively achieved by effectively carrying value forward from past earnings that occurred amid a stronger operating environment.
Source: CARD (2018) .
These asset sales have been necessary because of the large debt load that Pacific Ethanol took on when it acquired Aventine. This left it with quarterly interest expenses of roughly $4 million that have left its operating cash flows excluding changes to working capital low or even negative (see table) over the last four quarters as well as in FY 2017. While not captured by EBITDA, the company's occasional reliance on asset sales to meet its interest expenses partially explains why its book value has continued to decline over time: the Aventine acquisition, which was intended to give Pacific Ethanol access to higher-margin operating capacity, has instead been unable to even cover the costs of the acquisition when margins are especially low. Its book value will continue to decline in the current operating environment, even ignoring quarterly depreciation of another $10 million, due to its interest expenses alone.

In sum, two factors explain why Pacific Ethanol's book value is misleading as a long indicator. First, on an EBITDA basis the company's ethanol facilities have generated an average of $0.04/gallon since the Aventine acquisition took place and only $0.02/gallon in 2017 and 2018 to date. If Pacific Ethanol was able to sell its facilities for even 9x EBITDA of its post-Aventine average then it would still raise only $217.8 million compared to a book value of $329 million at the end of Q3. Second, the Aventine acquisition caused Pacific Ethanol's debt load to increase sharply to the point at which its total interest expenses have comprised a substantial fraction of its EBITDA. This debt load has in turn caused Pacific Ethanol's EV, or the cost of fully acquiring the company, to also remain substantially higher at the end of Q3 at $282.9 million than a 6x EBITDA purchase price would obtain. This latter multiple would be comparable to what Valero paid for GPRE's top-quality ethanol facilities ($1/gallon at a time when such facilities are recording average of EBITDAs of $0.17/gallon - see discussion below).
To be conservative when valuing Pacific Ethanol's shares I am adjusting its EV by treating its inventories at the end of Q3 of $56.2 million, which are currently comprised of easily sold commodities in the ethanol supply chain, as cash. This is based on the fact that the company has already been selling its inventory. This further assumes that the company's reported inventory value at the end of Q3 is correct, but it should be noted that the price of ethanol has experienced substantial volatility in Q4 to date. I calculate an EV at the time of writing of $213.5 million (see table), with the difference from the company's formal EV being that I am treating its inventory value as cash.

I calculate on the basis of these assumptions and its post-Aventine EBITDA/gallon that Pacific Ethanol's share price could fall much lower under current operating conditions without becoming undervalued. Specifically, the company's share price could fall to $0.02, resulting in a decline of 99% from the share price of $1.60 at the time of writing, before the EV would equal the $145.2 million purchase price under a 6x EBITDA acquisition scenario (see table). A 9x EBITDA multiple would be required to justify the current share price of $1.60. To put both of these acquisition scenarios in perspective, independent ethanol producers traded at 6x forward EBITDA in early 2007 following several ethanol producer IPOs. Pacific Ethanol would therefore need to find a buyer that was willing to wildly overpay before shareholders could expect to benefit. That seems unlikely given the operating environment that has prevailed in the ethanol sector over the last multiple quarters.

The pair trade
I use scenario analysis to illustrate why I consider a short position in Pacific Ethanol to be a useful hedge against a long position in REX. (There are 3.3 million Pacific Ethanol shares available to borrow according to Interactive Brokers .) Three scenarios are modeled. The optimistic scenario is one in which the U.S. biofuels mandate is strengthened to its statutory levels, improved trade relations cause U.S. ethanol exports to recover, and rising gasoline prices cause ethanol prices to rebound. 2014 exhibited these same conditions and the average sector production margin in that year was $0.67/gallon as a result. In that year Pacific Ethanol and REX American Resources recorded EBITDA of $0.16/gallon and $0.53/gallon, respectively. The two companies' shares also traded at roughly 6x trailing EV/EBITDA up until the broad retreat in energy market shares began in Q4 2014. Pacific Ethanol's and REX's share prices would appreciate by 531% and 126%, respectively, at that valuation level under those operating conditions (see table).

The pessimistic scenario, on the other hand, assumes that the conditions from the current TTM period prevail. The EV/EBITDA ratio remains at 6x but this scenario assumes that Pacific Ethanol and REX achieve EBITDAs of $0.02/gallon and $0.17/gallon, respectively. Pacific Ethanol's shares lose all of their value in this scenario due to its large debt load whereas REX, which has no long-term debt and only a small amount of short-term liabilities, experiences a share price decline of only 6% (see table). The pessimistic scenario is more likely to occur than optimistic scenario given that the former's operating conditions currently exist whereas the latter assumes that three major unexpected developments occur. The fact that Pacific Ethanol's share price still has value means that investors are treating it as a speculative long investment in anticipation of either a buyout or a return to 2014's conditions. The former can be discarded due to the acquisition value analysis conducted above whereas the latter is a low-probability event. Indeed, Pacific Ethanol's share price has recently exhibited the large volatility and steady declines that characterize speculative stocks.

Under the optimistic scenario investors would record a net return of 111% as the higher value of the REX shares (due to the higher share price) would more than offset the loss incurred by the short position as Pacific Ethanol's share price gained ground. While unlikely to occur, such conditions have prevailed in the current decade. The pessimistic scenario, in which ethanol's operating conditions remain the same as in 2017 and 2018, would result in a net loss of 3% as the short position in Pacific Ethanol largely offset the long position in REX. Finally, the baseline scenario, in which ethanol's operating conditions resemble those of 2016, would result in a net return of 25% as the long position in REX more than offset the negative impact of the short position in Pacific Ethanol. Of the three scenarios I consider the baseline scenario to be the most likely to occur since only one of the policy shifts described above would be a necessary prerequisite. The fact that the net loss is limited under the pessimistic scenario makes this an asymmetrical investment opportunity.

Conclusions
Policy uncertainty continues to prevail in the U.S. ethanol sector as the Trump administration's historical hostility to the U.S. biofuel blending mandate is expected to come under pressure as Mr. Trump's 2020 re-election campaign begins. Independent ethanol producers have historically seen their share prices record large double-digit (and even triple-digit) increases in response to favorable policy developments that have occurred following periods of extended low margins. One way for investors to gain exposure to this possible outcome is by initiating a long position in REX American Resources, which is one of the sector's highest-margin independent producers that is backed by a very strong balance sheet. Even this company's share price has experienced large losses under the type of conditions that have prevailed over the last year, however, and the possibility that no favorable policy developments will be forthcoming make it important that investors have an adequate hedge.
Such a hedge is available in the form of a short position in lower-margin independent ethanol producer Pacific Ethanol. That company made a large and ill-timed acquisition in late 2014, and the resulting financing costs from that acquisition have been a severe earnings headwind at a time when the ethanol sector's margins are trading near multi-year lows. The company's share price, which has already experienced large losses this year, is at continued risk in the event that prevailing operating conditions continue into 2019. Indeed, barring a major improvement in production margins, it is hard to envision a scenario that does not end in the company's share price approaching zero. This includes one in which its assets are acquired by a larger competitor.
An asymmetrical investment opportunity is available for investors in the form of a pair trade that comprises a long position in REX and a short position in Pacific Ethanol. REX's share price is trading at its lowest valuation of the current fiscal year due to the sector's prevailing low production margins but can expect to increase by 31% or more if one or more favorable policy developments occurs next year. The company's ability to achieve profitable operations even when the sector's margins are low and strong balance sheet provide downside protection at the same time. Pacific Ethanol's share price, on the other hand, can be expected to incur large losses in the event that current operating conditions continue to prevail (or worsen) due to its low production margins relative to the sector and deteriorating balance sheet. While REX's share price can be expected to experience a modest decline if operating conditions do not improve, this would be mostly offset by a paired short position in Pacific Ethanol. The pair trade offers investors a net return of 25% in the event that sector margins return to 2016 levels and a net return of 111% if sector margins return to 2014 levels.
